lead.headline: In Abu Dhabi Ukraine Talks, Security Guarantees Come First and Territory Last
lead.deck: Russia and Ukraine met face to face for the first time since February; European governments held a separate track with Kyiv.
body: Delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday 10 November. It was the first face-to-face meeting of Russian and Ukrainian officials since February, when the first US-brokered trilateral round was held in Geneva. That process has produced some prisoner-of-war exchanges and short, local ceasefires, but no settlement.

Each side sent senior figures. Ukraine’s team is led by Rustem Umerov and Russia’s by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, while US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner act as mediators. Representatives of the UK, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission met Ukraine’s team separately. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stressed that the Abu Dhabi talks are trilateral, and France said that there can be no lasting peace without addressing European security.

The agenda runs in a deliberate order. A US official said security guarantees would be central, possibly including a defence commitment modelled on Article 5 of NATO’s founding treaty, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. Any agreement on territory would most likely come last, after a post-war security framework is settled.

Territory is where the gap is widest. Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea. Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border; President Vladimir Putin wants all of Ukraine’s Donbas region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the first day “constructive and quite substantive”, but analyst Ilya Timtchenko of the Center for European Policy Analysis said: “you’re not really going to be seeing any deal.”

map.title: WHERE THE TALKS ARE HELD
map.caption: Talks between Russia and Ukraine, mediated by the US, are held in Abu Dhabi, far from the front line.

lead.why: The order of the agenda matters: settling security guarantees before borders tests whether outside powers will commit to defending Ukraine, which shapes what each side can accept on territory.

world.headline: Brazil Takes Its Fossil-Fuel Roadmap to COP31, and India and Nigeria Back It
world.deck: The plan is voluntary, sitting outside the formal negotiations in Antalya.
body: COP31, the United Nations climate conference, opened on 9 November in Antalya, Turkey, and runs until 20 November with nearly 200 countries expected. Turkey hosts the summit while Australia presides over the negotiations. On the second day the energy transition, the shift away from fossil fuels, was the central focus.

That day, COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago of Brazil presented a global roadmap on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, covering the phase-out of coal, oil and gas. It invites countries to draft national plans for clean energy systems by 2028, with the main push to cut coal, oil and gas envisaged after 2031. Countries would identify for themselves how much they depend on fossil fuels.

Big fossil-fuel users including India, Nigeria and Germany backed it. India, the world’s third-largest oil consumer and second-largest coal user, said the transition “must be co-created” and warned against swapping one dependency for another. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said all countries should start cutting fossil fuels by 2028. Some producer nations, however, are expected to resist writing the roadmap into the summit’s formal decisions. The chair of the Africa Group of Negotiators, Antwi-Boasiako Amoah of Ghana, said the transition must be just, with flexible timelines for fossil-dependent African nations and support with finance and technology.

Turkey is promoting its own voluntary target: raising electricity’s share of world energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. India’s Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said India will not sign that pledge. Money is the other fault line: the UN says developing countries need $305 billion a year by 2035 to adapt to climate change, nearly 10 times what they now receive. Former US climate envoy John Kerry said current policies are leading to 2.8C of warming. The United States, which formally left the Paris Agreement at the start of 2026, sent no official government delegation.

india.headline: Goyal Says India Is on Track for $1 Trillion in Exports, With $476 Billion in the First Half
india.deck: The commerce minister calls the target “sacrosanct” and points to an EU deal by March or April.
body: India’s Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said in New Delhi on Tuesday 10 November that the country is on track to meet its target of $1 trillion, or $1,000 billion, in exports in the current financial year, 2026-27. Exports here means goods and services together. “Our USD 1 trillion export target this year is sacrosanct,” he said. “We have to achieve it.”

The official numbers support the first half of that claim. Ministry of Commerce and Industry data show combined merchandise and services exports of $476.20 billion for April to September, up 13.84% from $418.31 billion a year earlier; Goyal rounded this to about $480 billion and said 48% of the target had been reached. Goods did most of the work: merchandise exports rose 18.51% to $259.89 billion, while services exports grew 8.69% to $216.31 billion. Excluding petroleum products, exports rose 15.56% to $218.70 billion, a sign that the growth is not just a story of fuel prices.

Reaching the goal depends on a stronger second half, and Goyal argued that “the first six months are normally less than the next six months.” Imports are rising too: they reached $551.13 billion, so the overall trade deficit, the gap between what India buys and sells abroad, widened to $74.93 billion from $58.10 billion. Services ran a surplus of $102.71 billion. September showed the same pattern: electronic goods exports jumped 70.44% to $5.31 billion, engineering goods rose 20.91% to $12.17 billion, and the month’s trade deficit narrowed to $13.30 billion from $14.17 billion as gold imports fell 81.27%. October’s figures are due on 15 November, and Goyal promised “a surprise”.

Trade agreements are central to the plan. Goyal said the 27-nation European Union market could become accessible to Indian goods at zero duty by March or April, and that negotiations with another seven or eight countries are under way. Once these deals are in place, he said, India will have preferential access to almost 75% of global GDP.

He also pointed to investment. European car manufacturers, he said, see India as a potential base for building cars for both the domestic and international markets, and Japanese companies are exploring billion-dollar partnerships with Indian manufacturers. Goyal spoke at the curtain-raiser for the Bharat Mobility Global Expo 2027, which expects about one million visitors. Goyal said the expo “will become the world’s largest in size” and suggested aiming for at least 25,000 international visitors.

politics_and_civics.headline: After Losing the House, Republicans Elect Jim Jordan as Their Leader by Secret Ballot
politics_and_civics.deck: He beat Steve Scalise 106-73; Democrats’ Hakeem Jeffries is the favourite for speaker.
body: In the US House of Representatives, each party chooses its own leaders, and the result of an election changes their titles. On Tuesday 10 November, one week after losing their majority in the midterm elections, House Republicans met behind closed doors and elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their leader for the next Congress. In a secret ballot he defeated the current Majority Leader, Steve Scalise of Louisiana, by 106 votes to 73.

Jordan, 62, has spent two decades in Congress. He chairs the House Judiciary Committee, helped found the House Freedom Caucus and is a top ally of President Donald Trump. “I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook,” he said. His win marks a change of course: in 2018 he lost a challenge for minority leader to Kevin McCarthy, 159-43, and Scalise is a close ally of Speaker Mike Johnson who has held leadership posts since John Boehner was speaker. Republicans also kept Tom Emmer of Minnesota as whip, the official who counts and gathers votes, after he beat August Pfluger of Texas.

The change at the top follows the scale of the defeat. Republicans lost more than 40 House seats, and Speaker Mike Johnson, who took the post in October 2023, announced the day after the midterms that he would step down from the leadership team. Democrats won roughly 260 seats, which NBC News described as the largest majority in 35 years.

In the new House, the majority party’s leader is expected to become speaker, who runs the chamber, while the minority leader speaks for the other side. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is the favourite for speaker. He needs 218 votes on the House floor on 3 January and can lose about 40 Democrats and still get there; he said Democrats are “confident that we will get to that number and beyond.” House Democrats choose their team next week, with Jeffries, Katherine Clark, Pete Aguilar and Ted Lieu unopposed for the top four posts.

The Senate follows the same pattern. Republicans voted on their leaders on Tuesday, with Majority Leader John Thune running unopposed to become minority leader. Senate Democrats will elect their leaders in early December, and Chuck Schumer is the favourite for majority leader.

economics.headline: Brent Crude Slips Below $90 as Trump Calls the Iran War “Effectively Over”
economics.deck: The benchmark is about 25% below its late-October peak, but diesel stays tight.
body: Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell to $89.70 a barrel in early European trading on Tuesday 10 November, its first time below $90 since August. WTI, the US benchmark, traded below $85, down more than 2%. Brent had already fallen 17% in the previous week, its largest weekly drop since the COVID-era turmoil of 2020, and it now stands about 25% below a late-October peak above $117.

Politics drove the move. On Monday, after meeting Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, a key mediator, President Donald Trump said Iran “militarily, is effectively over” and that further strikes were “quite unlikely”, though US forces were “locked and loaded”. Hopes for an end to the eight-month-old conflict have grown since the US midterm elections.

Tehran disputes the story. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi denied any meeting was planned, and Iran says it will not negotiate until Washington meets its “seven conditions”. Iranian officials said US strikes were continuing, with Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz reportedly hit overnight, and tanker attacks in the strait continued during the week, though traders looked past them. Analyst Tim Waterer of KCM Trade told Reuters the attacks “have not escalated in a way that has forced a fresh risk premium into the market”. Reports also said the US was open to letting Iran enrich uranium to almost 4%, but neither side has confirmed this.

Supply is recovering unevenly. A Reuters survey found OPEC output rose by 1.38 million barrels a day in October to 22.87 million, still below February’s 25.48 million. Saxo Bank’s Ole Hansen said crude flows have almost returned to pre-war levels, but gas and refined fuel supplies remain limited, which keeps prices high, particularly for diesel. Risks remain elsewhere in the region: Houthi fighters attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, causing what the Saudi energy ministry called a “limited fire” that was put out.

science_and_technology.headline: A Blood Signal Points to Ovarian Cancer’s Earliest, Precancerous Stage
science_and_technology.deck: In a test group it caught 92.3% of cases, but it is not yet ready for clinics.
body: Researchers at Hoag, a nonprofit health system in California, reported in the journal Nature Medicine on 10 November a blood-based warning signal for an early, precancerous stage of high-grade serous ovarian cancer. The study, led by Dr Rajan Gogna and Dr Esha Madan, was the result of an eight-year international effort. “Ovarian cancer does not begin the day we discover a tumor,” Gogna said.

The stage they targeted is called serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma, or STIC, which forms in the fallopian tube and may come 6 to 7 years before invasive cancer. It is precancerous: microscopic and not yet invading nearby tissue. That makes it hard to find. STIC cannot be seen on imaging, is missed by conventional cancer blood tests and is usually discovered by chance during surgery. Ovarian cancer is usually diagnosed only after it has spread; more than 320,000 women are diagnosed worldwide each year and more than 207,000 die from it.

The signal is an RNA molecule the team calls Tu-Stroma. Earlier work by the group found that cancer cells release tiny bubbles called extracellular vesicles, which carry Tu-Stroma to neighbouring healthy cells and weaken them, a process known as “cell competition”. The new study measured Tu-Stroma in vesicles in the blood of 506 people, including 43 with isolated STIC, 232 with high-grade serous cancer and 143 healthy controls, and found it raised in women with STIC and early-stage cancer. It separated STIC from healthy women with an accuracy score of 0.99, against 0.59 for CA125, today’s standard blood marker. In a separate validation group, the test detected STIC in 92.3% of women who had it and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women.

The authors stress the limits. The study used blood samples collected earlier from women whose diagnoses were already known, and the test has not been clinically validated. The share of positive results that would be correct ranges from about 16% in a lower-risk setting to about 72% in a high-risk group, and Gogna warned that a negative result “cannot currently exclude STIC”. That caution has history: large trials of CA125 testing, with or without ultrasound, did not reduce deaths from ovarian cancer. Next come studies that collect blood from women and follow them over time, including women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene changes, who face a higher risk and often weigh surgery to remove the fallopian tubes and ovaries. Such surgery can bring early menopause, which is why Madan said that for women at high risk, the work “could transform how we approach prevention.”

explainer.title: What is a security guarantee?
body: A security guarantee is a promise by one or more countries to help defend another if it is attacked. The best-known example is Article 5 of NATO’s founding treaty, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all members.

Ukraine is not a member of NATO, which is why the form and strength of any promise matter so much in the talks. A guarantee can range from a binding commitment to defend, as in Article 5, to looser pledges of weapons, money or consultation.

Guarantees differ in who promises and what they promise. In Abu Dhabi, the US has raised a commitment modelled on Article 5, while European governments are meeting Ukraine separately and say no lasting peace is possible without addressing Europe’s own security.

body: Nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31. It is a UN meeting about climate.
